record.title: TopKLoRA paper reports sparse causal circuits for removing known-trigger backdoors
record.summary: A new preprint presents TopKLoRA, a sparse fine-tuning adapter, with a Contrastive Latent Circuit Discovery pipeline for locating behaviors introduced during fine-tuning. In synthetic sleeper-backdoor model organisms up to 7B parameters, the authors report that ablating a selected circuit removes nearly all held-out responses to a known syntactic trigger, while multi-layer adapters retain benign instruction-following. The study compares against dense LoRA and reports smaller, more specific circuits. These are author-reported results in a controlled setup; unknown or semantic triggers, larger models, and independent reproduction remain open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report TopKLoRA and their Contrastive Latent Circuit Discovery (CLCD) pipeline identify and ablate necessary-and-sufficient circuits for a synthetically implanted backdoor with a known syntactic trigger in Gemma-2-2B, Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B model organisms. In their setup, ablation removed at least 99.9% of held-out triggered responses in each organism, while multi-layer adapters retained instruction-following close to clean twins.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors' matched-placement, rank-matched study, TopKLoRA circuits were smaller than dense-LoRA circuits across the reported 30 seed-matched pairs; their reported minimum circuit fraction was 1.2–6.8% of the TopKLoRA latent pool for eliminating the backdoor, compared with 20.6–38.9% for dense LoRA.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the authors' TopKLoRA/CLCD results was found or performed in this activation.
The paper's circuit search requires knowledge of the trigger and contrastive eliciting/control prompts; it does not test unknown or semantic triggers.
The reported base models reach 7B parameters and are controlled model organisms; transfer to larger or deployed models is not measured.
Different discovery orders can yield multiple verified circuits; the paper reports that circuits are minimal under a search grid rather than unique mechanisms.

brief.importance_rationale: If the paper's bounded results reproduce, sparse adapters with causal circuit tests could make certain fine-tuning backdoors easier to localize and remove while retaining benign task behavior; this could materially affect safety evaluation methods, but the evidence remains a small-model synthetic study.
limitations: All performance and causal-ablation results are author-reported in an arXiv preprint; independent reproduction was not performed.
Experiments use synthetic backdoors with explicit known syntactic triggers and contrastive trigger/control prompt pairs, unlike many realistic unknown-trigger cases.
The largest reported base model is 7B; generalization to larger or deployed systems is not established.
The paper does not interpret individual latents and acknowledges that multiple verified circuits may exist.
brief.summary: A new preprint presents TopKLoRA, a sparse fine-tuning adapter, with a Contrastive Latent Circuit Discovery pipeline for locating behaviors introduced during fine-tuning. In synthetic sleeper-backdoor model organisms up to 7B parameters, the authors report that ablating a selected circuit removes nearly all held-out responses to a known syntactic trigger, while multi-layer adapters retain benign instruction-following. The study compares against dense LoRA and reports smaller, more specific circuits. These are author-reported results in a controlled setup; unknown or semantic triggers, larger models, and independent reproduction remain open.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report synthetic known-trigger backdoor circuits in three model families up to 7B, with near-complete removal on held-out triggered prompts and close instruction-following retention for multi-layer adapters. They report smaller circuits than matched dense-LoRA controls.
technical.demonstrated_result: No independent result is demonstrated in this activation. The directly inspected evidence is an author-reported preprint and a public repository page; neither code nor training results were independently executed.
technical.mechanism: TopKLoRA applies a ReLU bottleneck and retains only the k largest adapter latents per token. CLCD ranks those latents using contrastive prompts, then verifies candidate circuits by testing both necessity (zero-ablation removes the behavior) and sufficiency (the selected circuit alone preserves it) on held-out prompts.
technical.regime: Fine-tuned open model organisms: Gemma-2-2B and Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B; backdoor inserted into 10,500 instruction examples using a 4.76% poisoned subset and an explicit known syntactic trigger; held-out prompt splits; circuit discovery uses known-trigger and control-prompt pairs.
technical.reproducibility: The paper states code is supplied for data generation, training, evaluation and circuit discovery, and a public GitHub repository page exposes experiment/config/source/test directories. This activation did not pin a commit, download weights/data, run code, or reproduce results.
technical.strongest_baseline: Rank-matched dense LoRA adapters at corresponding placement and training data; the paper also uses random latent-order and random-ablation controls.

brief.title: TopKLoRA paper reports sparse causal circuits for removing known-trigger backdoors
brief.why_it_matters: If reproduced beyond this controlled setting, the method could provide a more targeted way to audit and remove certain fine-tuning backdoors without broadly degrading benign task behavior. The result concerns synthetic known-trigger model organisms and does not establish protection against real-world or unknown-trigger backdoors.
